newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao makes silent trial appearance.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao makes silent trial appearance.

text.p: Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao appeared in a heavily-guarded makeshift court on Wednesday to face criminal charges, his first trial appearance in a string of legal cases that have shaken Indian politics.
Plainclothes commandos ushered Rao, 75, from a bullet-proof car to an annexe at New Delhi's Vigyan Bhavan conference hall to face charges in a seven-year-old criminal forgery case.
Raising his clasped hands in the Indian greeting, Rao bowed to photographers before entering the squat building.
In the windowless courtroom, Rao was flanked by four bodyguards and sat apart from three co-accused in the case, including an ex-minister and a Hindu guru.

Rao remained impassive and silent while his lawyer R.K. Anand argued that the charges, which carry a maximum sentence of seven years in jail, were "fabricated" and appealed for bail to protect the former prime minister against arrest.
Rao, who had been exempted from having to attend the trial hearing but came anyway, left the court room after three and a half hours as the judge called a luncheon break.

His lawyer said Rao did not plan to return for the afternoon session but would attend the continuation of the hearing on Thursday. It was not known whether chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar would rule on the bail request on Thursday when the hearing was set to resume.
Rao is the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges.

Rao's appearance at the trial hearing capped weeks of legal manoeuvring in a tangled web of cases that have undercut his authority within the Congress party, which suffered a humiliating defeat in general elections in April and May.

He resigned in disgrace as Congress chief in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a separate criminal cheating case. But he remains head of Congress's parliamentary delegation and retains political clout.
His influence is magnified by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's dependence on Congress support to help thwart potential challenges from right-wing Hindu nationalists in parliament.
Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition does not control an outright majority in parliament and needs Congress's backing.
Rao's legal woes have compounded his party's misfortunes following its worst defeat ever in the general elections and stirred tension between Congress and Deve Gowda's United Front.

But financial markets, which lost substantial ground last month as Rao's worries began to shake the government, have largely discounted the prospect of the eventual demise of the political leader who ushered in market-friendly economic reforms.

The small, carpeted courtroom -- chosen by police as a substitute venue considered more secure than crowded local courts -- was filled with two dozen reporters and Congress leaders. No TV cameras or photographers were allowed.
Congress general secretary Ghulam Nabi Azad and former cabinet ministers Pranab Mukherjee and V.C. Shukla attended the hearing, dominated by arguments over bail.

Rao remained silent and expressionless as his lawyer, Anand, argued that his client should be given bail. On October 9 another court granted Rao temporary bail which protects him against arrest, but the order expires on November 6.
At issue are charges filed by federal police that Rao was alleged to have conspired in 1989 to defame V.P. Singh, a Congress rebel who later became prime minister.
"The entire case against me is motivated and fabricated," said Anand, speaking for a silent Rao. "There is no case against me."
